parts.title: We Sealed Bread in a Bag for 10 Days. What GREW? (Part 1) | Fungi
parts.description:
We sealed one slice of bread in a bag for ten days. Something grew! Be a spore and find out how bread mould gets its food. Part 1 of Primary 3 Science, Diversity: fungi and bacteria (a mushroom is NOT a plant).

In this part:
• Bread mould: a fungus that grows on bread
• Be a spore: how fungi get their food (they absorb it)
• A mushroom's cap, stalk and gills: fungi reproduce through spores
• Useful or harmful fungi: mushrooms, yeast, tempeh and bread mould

Key words: bread mould, absorb, spores, yeast.
Watch Part 2: your hands look clean. What is living on them?

Did you know? In 1928 Alexander Fleming noticed that mould in one of his dishes had stopped bacteria from growing. From that mould came penicillin, a medicine that stops harmful bacteria from growing.

TheOneApp, Explained: Singapore primary science, made fun. Play along with Pip, Basil and Momo: show fingers to lock in, keep score on your hand, beat the Buddies! Practise this topic in TheOneApp.

Singapore Primary 3 Science (2023 syllabus): Diversity, classification of living things: fungi and bacteria (Chapter 2, pp. 34–44; Let's Apply Q3, p. 42; What I Have Learnt and the concept map, pp. 43–44). Also fits US NGSS 2-LS4-1 (Grade 2 to 3).
Try it at home: find one food at home made with a useful fungus or useful bacteria (bread, tempeh, yoghurt) and show someone at home. Never touch or sniff mould. Wash your hands with soap before you eat.
Singapore and the US: tempeh at the nasi padang stall is made with a useful fungus, and yoghurt drinks at the school canteen have useful bacteria. In the US (Grade 3), yeast makes pizza dough rise, and a mushroom may pop up in the backyard after rain. Look, do not pick.

parts.title: Your Hands LOOK Clean. What Is Living on Them? (Part 2) | Bacteria
parts.description:
They look clean. So what is living on them? Shrink down and be a bacterium on a fingertip at recess. Part 2 of Primary 3 Science, Diversity: fungi and bacteria.

In this part:
• A microscope: how we see bacteria
• Rod-shaped, sphere-shaped and spiral-shaped bacteria
• Be a bacterium: why we wash our hands with soap before we eat
• Are all bacteria harmful? Useful bacteria in yoghurt
• Showdown: read every column (spores alone do not decide)
• The whole chapter on one map, and the Exam corner

Key words: microscope, harmful, useful.
Watch Part 1 first! Next episode: materials. What is your snack box made of?
